result:
Understood. I'll keep this to one choice about how to build it, and then I'll write it up.

**Approach 1 (my recommendation): add it to the taproom app.**
- Batch tracking goes into the Flask app that already runs your tabs, as its own section with its own tables in the same SQLite database on the Pi.
- Brewers open a page on a phone or tablet. They scan sack lot numbers with a USB or Bluetooth barcode scanner.
- One app runs, one database gets backed up, and the brewers use one login.
- The cost is that a bad update to the tabs code could also take down batch tracking, and the other way around.

**Approach 2: a separate small app on the same Pi.**
- It has its own database file and its own address.
- Tabs and trace records can't break each other.
- The cost is two apps to start, update, and back up.

**Dropped: off-the-shelf brewery software** (for example, Ekos or Breww). These products already do traceability. But they cost a monthly fee, they don't build on what you have, and your label printer may not work with them.

I recommend Approach 1. The app is small and runs on one Pi, so one app and one backup is the simpler life. I'll keep the batch code in its own section so it stays easy to separate later.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Most barcode scanners act like a keyboard. They "type" the lot number and press Enter. So a normal web form takes scans with no special driver, which suits wet hands.
- Flask can hold a separate feature in a "blueprint," a self-contained group of pages. Approach 1 can keep batch tracking walled off inside the same app.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

This is project-sized. I'll write it as a design document. A reviewer will read it first, and I may come back once with a few questions. The folder isn't under git yet, so I'll also ask before I set that up.

Which approach do you want, 1 or 2?
